blocks: An automated serial sectioning technique is used to create the three-dimensional reconstructions. Serial sections are taken at 4.75 μm intervals. A digital image is recorded of each section and the exact position of the sample is noted. The groups of images are then cleaned, the threshold adjusted to clearly distinguish the liquid-eutectic interface, and layered in sequence. Using the positioning data, an area common to all images in the sequence is then selected to account for any misalignment during the image capturing procedure. The resized images are finally stacked and aligned before being run through Interactive Data Language (IDL) software for the three-dimensional reconstruction.

Once the dendritic microstructure is reconstructed, the proposed analyses are undertaken. To quantitatively determine the presence of any preferential directionality or symmetry of the interfacial orientations, surface normal vectors are utilized in a stereographic projection of the microstructure. A stereographic projection is a graphical technique that converts three-dimensional angular information into two two-dimensional images. First, the interface of the reconstruction is triangulated into millions of patches, each with a unique normal vector, n. Now, considering the reconstruction completely enclosed by a theoretical reference sphere (Fig. 2), normal vectors from each triangulated patch can be projected out from the structure until it intersects the surface of the sphere at a set of points called poles. A projection plane tangent to the reference sphere and perpendicular to the growth direction (z-axis) illustrates the intersection of each pole on a hemisphere. Two complimentary hemispheres together comprise the entire three-dimensional reference sphere. Plotting the frequency at which poles of equal orientation intersect the projection plane transforms the stereographic projection into a probability distribution plot. By observing trends in these orientation distributions, the directionality of the microstructural interfaces can be visualized. Consequently, any symmetry will be resolved through this process.

Due to the morphological variation present during coarsening, a morphology independent measure of the microstructure, interfacial curvature, is required for sufficient assessment and comparison of dendritic evolution. Interfacial curvature may be gauged through the analysis of two parameters, the mean curvature, H, and the Gaussian curvature, K:

As discussed in the MOTIVATION, the mean curvature, H, determines the solute concentration at the interface under the Gibbs-Thompson equation (Eqn.1). As material concentration changes, so will the mean curvature. The time derivative of mean and Gaussian curvatures are proportional, thus it is applied as an additional measure.³ The importance of the Gaussian curvature is also illustrated by a saddle-shaped surface in which the principle radii of a surface (identified in Fig. 3) are exact opposites, R₁ = -R₂. In this case, Eqn. 3 yields H = 0, thus making the interfacial solute concentration equal to that of a planar interface, despite the interface not resembling such a physical orientation. Therefore, it is necessary to measure both the mean and Gaussian curvatures in order to characterize the true interfacial orientation.²
